newsitem.title: THAILAND: More defaults seen in Thai debt market.
newsitem.headline: More defaults seen in Thai debt market.

text.p: Thailand's failing economic health and plunging stock market are expected to precipitate more defaults on debt repayments by local corporate borrowers, analysts said on Wednesday.

Several corporate borrowers, mostly in the ailing property sector, have struggled since late last year to meet debt repayment obligations because the country's sustained economic slowdown has prevented them from achieving revenue targets.

"As the tide ebbs, it exposes...debris underneath the water," an international fixed income fund manager said, adding that she did not expect a recent series of Thai corporate debt defaults to pass soon.
The Bank of Thailand has projected that the Thai economy will expand 5.9 percent this year, its slowest pace in a decade after 6.4 percent growth in 1996 and 8.7 percent in 1995.
The property sector, in its fourth year of a slump, has shaken an overexposed finance sector, driving cash-strapped financial institutions to the verge of insolvency.
The Thai stock exchange has lost 57 percent of its value in the past year with the market index languishing at its eight year low of 557 points on Wednesday.

Recent debt defaults or loan restructuring came mostly from property firms including Natural Park Plc, Somprasong Land Plc, and unlisted condominium builder Sahaviriya City Plc, as well as by investment firm One Holding Plc and furniture maker STA Group.
An analyst at Asia Equity Thailand Ltd said other property firms scrambling to meet debt financing needs were Bangkok Land Plc, Juldis Develop Plc and Property Perfect Plc.

"We should see more defaults in the near future but how many more will partly depend on how much interest rates decline and how slow the economy recovers," said an investment bank officer at Krungthai Thanakit Plc.

Thai companies have about 90 outstanding Eurobond issues in six different currencies. Most of them were floated during Thailand's boom years in 1993 and 1994 when its companies found it much cheaper to borrow abroad than at home.
Most of these Euro-convertible debentures (ECDs) are unsecured but carry put options that give holders a right to redeem their investment before the papers mature.
The Thai private sector accounts for about 80 percent of the country's total $91.7 billion in foreign debt.
Analysts said Bangkok Land faced obligations of making a $675,000 interest payment on its $150 million ECD in October and it would be required to repay a 22 million Swiss franc loan in November.
They said although Bangkok Land's $150 milion ECD would not mature until October 2003, its holders would likely choose to redeem the investment early by exercising their put options in October 1998.
Bangkok Land's profit plunged to 7.4 million baht ($296,000) in the year ended March 31, 1997, from 608.2 million a year ago.

Analysts said Bangkok Land, like all property firms, posted a tiny pre-sale revenue as home buyers had delayed or refused to honour contracts of paying up home prices amid a prolonged bearish trend faced by the industry.
Few analysts expected a quick turnaround in the sluggish economy. They said business and finance sector performance would likely to get worse before it got better.
An indication that property developers and some finance firms were desperate for cash could be found in surging domestic corporate bond yields.

"You could easily buy domestic corporate bonds of property and finance firms with 20-30 percent yields. The offers reflect how much these companies are short of cash," a fixed income fund manager said.
